planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering finishes.

directions: Mohawk is a US National Arboretum introduction bred specifically to combine strong fragrance with outstanding fall color, two traits rarely found together in one viburnum. Dark red buds open in mid-spring to white, waxy, spicy clove-scented flower clusters that rival Korean spice viburnum for perfume but on a more vigorous, disease-resistant plant. Glossy dark green summer foliage turns brilliant orange-red in fall, and Mohawk shows notably better resistance to bacterial leaf spot than many other Burkwood viburnum selections. Site it near a walkway or window where the spring fragrance can be enjoyed, and give it room to reach its full rounded size without crowding.

planting.note: Plant container stock in early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; avoid pruning until immediately after the spring bloom since flower buds form on old wood.

directions: Bred at the Arnold Arboretum from Viburnum carlesii x V. bitchiuense, Judd viburnum was developed to keep the intense, sweet fragrance of Korean spice viburnum while gaining better vigor and disease resistance. Pink buds open to fragrant white to pale-pink flower clusters in mid-spring, followed by red fruit that ripens to black and reddish-purple fall foliage. Its dense, rounded, symmetrical habit needs little pruning beyond the occasional light shaping right after flowering, making it a low-fuss choice for a fragrant foundation planting or mixed shrub border.

planting.note: Plant in spring in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to light shade, allowing generous space since this is one of the largest-growing viburnums; prune immediately after bloom since flowers form on old wood.

directions: Chinese snowball viburnum produces some of the largest flower clusters of any hardy landscape shrub, with sterile snowball-shaped heads 6 to 8 inches across opening lime-green in mid-spring before maturing to pure white. Because the flowers are sterile, the plant sets no fruit, trading wildlife berries for weeks of striking bloom display. It grows into a large, rounded, semi-evergreen shrub in the Gulf South (fully deciduous in colder zones) and works best as a specimen or large screening plant where its considerable mature size is an asset rather than a problem. Give it room, water it well while establishing, and resist heavy pruning except right after flowering.

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained, evenly moist soil sited with some afternoon shade in hot climates; two seedlings or clones are needed nearby for reliable berry set since fruiting requires cross-pollination.

directions: Leatherleaf viburnum is grown chiefly for its bold, coarse-textured evergreen foliage — long, deeply veined, corrugated dark green leaves with a felted gray-brown underside that give the shrub year-round structural presence. Flat clusters of creamy-white flowers open in late spring, followed by red berries that ripen to black by late summer if a second unrelated plant is present for cross-pollination. It makes an effective evergreen screen or backdrop shrub but tends to lose its lower leaves and look leggy with age, so it is best planted behind lower shrubs or perennials that can mask its base. Afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch in hot, sunny sites.

planting.note: Plant with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and shade or mulch the root zone while training the vine up a trellis or through a shrub into full sun; light pruning group, so remove only dead or weak stems in late winter.

directions: Bred in Poland by Władysław Noll, Niobe is one of the deepest, most saturated red large-flowered clematis cultivars widely grown, with velvety ruby-red 5 to 6 inch blooms set off by contrasting gold-yellow stamens that darken toward maroon as they age. It flowers heavily on old wood in late spring and early summer, then produces a lighter rebloom on new growth later in the season, so pruning should be light — just tidying and removing weak growth in late winter rather than a hard cutback. Like most clematis, it performs best with its roots kept cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun, a classic pairing achieved by underplanting with low groundcover or mulch.

planting.note: Plant with the crown a couple of inches below soil level, shading the root zone while the vine climbs a trellis, arbor, or fence into full sun; light pruning group — trim lightly in late winter rather than cutting hard to the ground.

directions: Introduced in England in 1876, The President remains one of the most reliable and widely planted large-flowered clematis more than a century later, prized for its rich purple-blue, star-shaped 5 to 6 inch flowers with contrasting reddish-purple stamens and silvery reverse petals that catch the light as they twist in the breeze. It reblooms twice in a season — a strong flush in late spring to early summer followed by a lighter repeat in late summer — and its long garden pedigree has earned it lasting popularity. As with other clematis, keep the roots cool and shaded (mulch or low companion planting works well) while the vine itself grows into full sun.

common_name: Diana Rose of Sharon (Sterile White Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood.

directions: Diana was introduced by the US National Arboretum as part of a breeding program aimed at improving on old-fashioned rose of sharon, and it remains one of the best white-flowered selections available. Its large, pure white, 4 to 5 inch flowers stay open later into the evening and remain open longer during the day than most rose of sharon cultivars, and as a sterile triploid it sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with older althea. Bloom runs from midsummer into fall on new wood, giving a long season of clean white color when many other shrubs have finished flowering; site it as a summer anchor in a mixed border or informal hedge.

common_name: Miss Molly Butterfly Bush (Sterile Raspberry-Red Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to about 12 inches to encourage vigorous new flowering growth.

directions: Miss Molly was bred at North Carolina State University as part of a program to produce sterile, non-seeding butterfly bushes that avoid the invasive spread of older Buddleja davidii selections. It produces dense, conical flower spikes in a true, deep raspberry-red to cherry-red color that is unusually saturated for the genus, blooming continuously from summer through frost with minimal deadheading needed since it sets almost no viable seed. Its more compact habit than species butterfly bush makes it easier to fit into smaller borders, and like all buddleja it draws butterflies and hummingbirds in large numbers once established. It tolerates heat and drought well once its root system is established.
sources: North Carolina State University JC Raulston Arboretum
